quick.summary: Why a clever control confused everyone, and when a familiar pattern is the better design.
quick.takeaway: Common task, common pattern. Invent only for a new task.

beats.line: I designed a dial for picking dates. Testers kept looking for a calendar. Why?
Because they have picked dates a thousand times, on a calendar.
But the dial is faster once you learn it.
Once you learn it. Most people will not stay to learn.
For a common task, use the pattern people already know.
Invent only when the task itself is new.

board.text: new task → a new pattern may fit

beats.line: Then spend your effort on the details. Sensible starting values, clear labels.
A calendar, opening on today, with next week one tap away.
Familiar, and still better than most.

quiz.question: When is designing a brand new interaction pattern most justified?
options: When the task itself is new to users
When the standard pattern looks boring
When a competitor uses the standard one
When there is spare time in the sprint
quiz.explanation: People bring habits from other products; a new pattern earns its learning cost only when no familiar one fits the task.

quiz.question: For a task people already do in many products, a familiar pattern is usually easier to use than a novel one.
quiz.explanation: People reuse what they have learned elsewhere, so a familiar pattern needs no learning.
